takes.mechanism: Hamstring injury on a quarterback who relies more than anyone on scrambling and off-script plays out of the pocket — the same pattern as Lamar Jackson's recent hamstring, where he was not the same player.

takes.why: 6 out of 10 panic — cut bait / sell for whatever you can, he is losing the job quickly.
takes.mechanism: He fumbled again (18 fumbles since 2021, most in the NFL), after which TreVeyon Henderson took 76% of backfield carries to his 24%, and with A.J. Brown out for four-plus more games defenses will keep loading the box.

takes.why: He is taking the backfield over — the buy side of the Rhamondre fade, though the loaded boxes cap the ceiling near-term.
takes.mechanism: In his return he took 16 carries, a 76-yard touchdown and 60% of snaps to Stevenson's 36%, and he has been the most explosive back in the backfield for two years.

takes.why: 5-7 out of 10 panic on a second-round pick — the role is not there yet even though he is the better back.
takes.mechanism: He played under 40% of snaps and ran only 26% of routes while Tyler Allgeier led the team in snaps and ran 58% of routes; Mike LaFleur said they will rotate, the rookie is still being eased back, and with Jacoby Brissett the team will play from behind where Love is not on the field.

takes.why: He is the passing-down/negative-script back in this backfield right now, which is the only role that scores with this team trailing.
takes.mechanism: Led the team in snaps and ran 58% of routes to Love's 26%.

takes.why: 10 out of 10 panic — bench him in 12-team leagues and he is a droppable/borderline cut in 10-to-12-team formats.
takes.mechanism: He is the fourth passing-game option: one catch on four targets across 62 routes, and last week 89% of routes for a 7% target share while Michael Wilson and Kendrick Bourne lapped him; his 6.9% targets-per-route-run ranks better than only Bryce Lance, Jakobi Meyers and Calvin Ridley among 90 WRs with 30+ routes. It is year three with no improvement.

takes.why: He has been the far better Cardinals receiver for two straight weeks and is being trusted — the cheap way to own this passing game.
takes.mechanism: Past experience with Mike LaFleur; last week he led the team at 20% of routes with a 19% target share while Harrison ran 89% of routes for 7%.

takes.why: Sell — and if you missed the three-touchdown window, sell the moment he posts another 12-14 point game over the next three weeks (Colts, Cowboys, Titans).
takes.mechanism: His role already flipped: 43% of carries and a 3% target share to Woody Marks' 57% and 11%, six carries for 10 yards at 1.7 per attempt, and he showed no explosiveness last year either (30th in explosive rate, 38th in broken tackles), which is why the Lions traded him.

takes.why: He has taken the lead in this backfield — the buy side of the Montgomery sell.
takes.mechanism: 57% of carries and an 11% target share in Week 2 versus Montgomery's 43% and 3%, with snaps now essentially even (48% to 52%) through two games.

takes.why: Number one wide receiver pickup of the week and arguably the number one overall add — be decently aggressive, this is the rookie breakout you chase.
takes.mechanism: Second-round rookie playing 90%-plus of snaps with a touchdown in each of his first two games (the only rookie WR besides Bucky Irving-era company: Abuka and Boston since 2000 in that split), a loud steady camp/preseason drumbeat from beat writers who said he might end up the team's WR1, and a big, physical touchdown-threat profile that matters most when you do not trust the quarterback.

takes.why: Mike's number one wide receiver add, ahead of Denzel Boston — the safer of the two in a tier of their own.
takes.mechanism: Better team, better quarterback and better offense than Cleveland; he is playing the snaps and running the routes, his yards per route run are outrageous, he has deep-ball touchdown equity, and targets should go up with Dallas Goedert hurt.

takes.why: Must be rostered in 100% of leagues and an absolute must-add if you own Kenneth Walker — add him NOW, not next week when he is a full FAAB dump.
takes.mechanism: He would inherit all the work if Walker went down, he already looks great, it is an offense they trust, and Andy Reid said that morning they want to give him more work because they do not want Walker carrying this workload; he could even be a double-flex start in a blowout script (Chiefs vs Miami this week).

takes.why: Spend only a few bucks of FAAB as a develop-later bet — unless you are the J.K. Dobbins manager, in which case make him a priority and pay up.
takes.mechanism: Rookie who was their number two RB in pre-draft rookie rankings, took over in the fourth quarter after Dobbins went down and out-snapped Tyler Badie to win the game; the cold water is Dobbins is reportedly fine, R.J. Harvey may be back, and Coleman still played only ~40% of snaps with both of them out for three quarters.
takes.faab: a few bucks / not going heavy; higher priority if you roster J.K. Dobbins

takes.why: Mike's stream of the week is 'the Seattle quarterback' — Darnold if he is back, Lock if not; it does not matter which.
takes.mechanism: Drew Lock is the highest-rated passer through two weeks and knows where to butter the bread — Jaxon Smith-Njigba is running a 44% target share and now draws Washington.

takes.why: Same stream — if he is back from the injury, fantastic; the Seattle QB job is the play regardless of occupant.
takes.mechanism: Mike McDonald said Darnold is on track to practice this week (return TBD), and the offense is feeding JSN a 44% target share against Washington.

takes.why: Worth adding as the number two streaming option this week — you could do worse off the waiver wire.
takes.mechanism: Cleared concussion protocol and will start Week 3 on the road at Tampa Bay; coming off a concussion historically does not impact production the way an ankle injury would, and Deshaun Watson just played fine against the Buccaneers.

takes.why: A great pickup if he is sitting on your wire — though Shough is better right now.
takes.mechanism: Stated only as 'Brock Purdy's good / Brock Purdy's a great pickup' in the context of leagues where both he and Shough were available.

takes.why: Not startable for at least two weeks; if your only path to Shough is dropping him, make that trade — otherwise roster both.
takes.mechanism: There are 12 other quarterbacks they would rather start both this week (at Jacksonville) and next (at Buffalo), and the bright days may not arrive until A.J. Brown is back, which they expect to be about six weeks.

takes.why: Named the Week 3 starter — he unlocks the Atlanta passing game and is worth adding, though he turns the ball over.
takes.mechanism: Falcons named him starter for Thursday night against Green Bay; Cooper Rush was objectively not playing starting-NFL-quarterback-quality football, so the first two weeks of Atlanta data should be thrown in the garbage.

takes.why: The top tight end add of the week — clearest path to volume of the three.
takes.mechanism: Charlie Kolar and David Njoku both went on IR, making him the TE1 from Week 3 on; he showed talent as a rookie, he is forced onto the field, and this offense needs another target beyond Ladd McConkey after outrageous drops from the rest of the room.

takes.why: If it is confirmed Puka Nacua needs hernia surgery he becomes the number one overall pickup of the week — over Denzel Boston, over Jonah Coleman; Puka and Davante Adams managers should pay up now.
takes.mechanism: He is the fill-in for Nacua's role (6-54-TD in Week 2 without him) and would be the number two option in that offense, meaning a tight end putting up wide receiver numbers; Adams is also old enough that his absence would open the same role.

takes.why: Worth adding purely as a touchdown play — one of the three tight ends worth a claim this week.
takes.mechanism: He has a nose for the end zone and is the goal-line weapon in a Carolina offense that is now throwing a ton, despite doing nothing else (17 and 33 yards the first two weeks).

takes.why: Only if you have gotten zero production from your tight end — no ceiling case, pure floor patch.
takes.mechanism: You cannot trust the other Pittsburgh pass catchers to catch the football (most drops in football), so targets funnel to him, but the next four matchups are Cincinnati, Cleveland, the Colts and Tampa Bay.

takes.why: The sneakiest play on the board — their WR3/WR4 add behind Boston and Wicks.
takes.mechanism: 12 targets and 6-63 last week, big passing volume in the Geno Smith offense on a team that will frequently be playing from behind, on the road in Detroit this week, and he gets the deep opportunities that will eventually connect.

takes.why: Andy's number two wide receiver add and a fine shot this week, but a genuinely tough weekly hold.
takes.mechanism: Kirk Cousins is playing very good football and Tucker has actual staying power, with a fast-paced matchup in New Orleans expected to produce a lot of points; the counter is that across four years he has produced only two or three big games a season and then disappears — and Jack Bech or Jalen Nailor could just as easily be the one who pops.

takes.why: The alternative Raiders lottery ticket — the pick Mike made over Tre Tucker in the fantasy time machine.
takes.mechanism: The Raiders are an environment where a wide receiver can pop off, and Tucker has a history of popping off then disappearing, so Bech was the more reliable version of the same bet.

takes.why: Break-glass-in-case-of-emergency starter this week only, not a rest-of-season play.
takes.mechanism: He looked good, but it depends entirely on whether DJ Moore is out — and DJ Moore is back soon.

takes.why: Same category as Keon Coleman — startable only if the starter ahead of him sits.
takes.mechanism: His value is entirely a function of whether Zay Flowers plays, and Flowers has a good shot to play Week 3 against the Cowboys.

takes.why: If you have to start one Miami replacement receiver this week, it is Washington over Chris Bell.
takes.mechanism: Caleb Douglas may miss time, and Chris Bell played only 41% of snaps, so Washington is clearly ahead right now.

takes.why: The better roster stash of the two Miami options even though Washington is the better start — upside over snaps.
takes.mechanism: By the same logic as the Denzel Boston argument (bet on the higher-ceiling young talent), Mike would rather roster Bell despite his 41% snap share.

takes.why: A real fit worth monitoring, but well down the list of adds.
takes.mechanism: Competent wide receiver with a history with Daniel Jones who can be 'Alec Pierce light' in an offense that badly needed somebody.

takes.why: If Saquon misses time, Bigsby is the one to own of the two — but expect a split, not a league-winning inheritance, so do not join the over-mad rush.
takes.mechanism: When Saquon left, Bigsby took the rushing work and Shipley took the passing work (near-inverse route and snap shares); Bigsby carries the touchdown upside and the Eagles should not be in that level of passing situation going forward.

takes.why: The lesser half of the Saquon contingency — passing-down work only.
takes.mechanism: He got the routes and shared the snaps while Bigsby took the carries; he also ran 100% of the two-minute offense in Week 1 and 21% of snaps.

takes.why: The one running back name on the board with any chance of being a pick-up-and-start guy.
takes.mechanism: He went 21 for 92 and should see more snaps, and Jadarian Price's shoulder injury plus a fumble could push the team to ride the hot hand.

takes.why: The backfield is settled — he is the man and the committee talk is over.
takes.mechanism: '1A, 1B is nonsense. It's Bucky' — the situation has shaken out, which is why Kenny Gainwell is now droppable (2 and 3 fantasy points).

takes.why: Drop him to make room for this week's adds.
takes.mechanism: Two and three fantasy points the last two weeks; the backfield has resolved to Bucky Irving.

takes.why: Not a must-drop but certainly a can-drop — stash on IR if you have the spot, otherwise move on.
takes.mechanism: Week-to-week groin injury with a rehab path, and it is hard to see him coming back to what he was.

takes.why: Drop him unless you have a completely empty IR slot — do not roster him for the next month.
takes.mechanism: He will attempt to rehab the heel and ankle to avoid surgery but is likely to be placed on IR; he struggled coming back from the surgery before, you cannot play him immediately on return, and re-aggravation risk is real — the bench spot is not worth the what-ifs.

takes.why: Listed as a drop candidate for this week's claims.
takes.mechanism: Named on the drop list without elaboration (the Giants quarterback room just collapsed with Jaxson Dart's MCL).

takes.why: Probably a drop.
takes.mechanism: Named on the drop list without elaboration, in a Chargers receiver room whose drops were outrageous.

takes.why: A drop — 'that's disgusting, but I don't think he's very good.'
takes.mechanism: Stated as a talent/quality judgment only.

takes.why: On the drop-candidate list and named their 'Meow Man of the year' through two weeks — an effort indictment, not just a usage one.
takes.mechanism: On film he is not putting in effort on the routes he is given and runs routes 'fully not expecting to get the ball'; the coaches' defense is legitimate (Trey McBride and Kendrick Bourne own the short middle, Marv is supposed to threaten downfield), but he is not playing like he wants the targets.

takes.why: A top-five player to drop if you have him.
takes.mechanism: His receivers lead football in drops (he is top five among quarterbacks in drops), and the next four matchups are Cincinnati, Cleveland, the Colts and Tampa Bay.

takes.why: Do not expect him to keep ascending — he is the tax you pay to own Denzel Boston, not a reason to buy the offense.
takes.mechanism: Asked directly whether he continues to ascend or improve, the answer was 'I do not — I would find that doubtful'; Cleveland has received the post-Seattle Russell Wilson version of him.

takes.why: Not the Browns rookie to chase — Boston is.
takes.mechanism: He is running around underneath (compared to DK Metcalf's rookie-year usage in Tennessee); with a quarterback you do not love you want the tackle-breaking, big-play, red-zone body instead.

takes.why: Week 1 worries are settled — he is still capable of being a true number one, and he gets even better without Puka.
takes.mechanism: 8 catches for 195 yards and two touchdowns for 35 fantasy points with Nacua out, plus a goal-line opportunity; the Week 1 Australia game was a travel/fatigue anomaly to throw out.

takes.why: Nothing needs to change — he is a locked weekly WR1 with a plus matchup against Washington.
takes.mechanism: A 44% target share; once a receiver reaches 30% target share he is almost guaranteed to be a fantasy WR1, and Drew Lock (highest-rated passer through two weeks) keeps feeding him.

takes.why: Big bounce back — he is going to be very, very good the rest of the season.
takes.mechanism: Week 2 was the perfect test (an average defense that can score, not a give-me team) and he answered with double-digit targets, 8 catches, 138 yards; the Week 1 Kansas City game goes in the garbage because KC shut down the Broncos too.

takes.why: Expect him back Week 3 against Dallas — a very nice matchup to return into.
takes.mechanism: He has a good shot to play in Week 3; the plan was always to rest one week against the Saints and get him back, and Dallas's defense looks worse and worse as data gathers.

takes.why: Week 3 is genuinely up for grabs and hernia surgery could be announced at any moment — handcuff him with Terrance Ferguson now.
takes.mechanism: Sean McVay is not sure he plays Week 3; the reports conflict between hip and groin, which is the sports-hernia/abdomen area, and he has a history of frequent injury problems (explicitly flagged as speculation, not reporting).

takes.why: He is fine this week and goes right back to being the guy — but his managers should be pre-buying Jonah Coleman because he cannot stay healthy.
takes.mechanism: Tom Pelissero reported he is good after the Week 2 scare; the concern is the injury-prone label, which they argue is real ('future injuries, one of the best predictors might be past injuries').

takes.why: His bell-cow workload is not sustainable and the team is actively planning to cut it — own Emmett Johnson as the hedge.
takes.mechanism: He is on pace for 535 opportunities, which is impossible, and Andy Reid said that morning they want to give Emmett Johnson more work because they do not want Walker carrying this level of workload.

takes.why: This is a real split, not a Kyren Williams show — Corum is roster-relevant.
takes.mechanism: Kyren Williams and Blake Corum were almost identical: 12 carries each, 85 yards for Kyren and 79 for Corum, with both involved in the receiving game (Kyren caught the receiving touchdown).

takes.why: He is going to miss time — the Giants' fantasy ecosystem collapses with him out.
takes.mechanism: Left MCL injury with an MRI scheduled; early report is he will miss some time.

takes.why: A situation to monitor, and a direct warning against the one-week overreaction that had him ranked over CeeDee Lamb after Week 1.
takes.mechanism: Shoulder popped out of place and was popped back in; he did not want to leave because Dart was already out, but effectively left for the rest of the game — and with Jameis Winston under constant duress he managed one catch for one yard.

takes.why: His return is the reason Shough could go from hot start to a truly special season — buy the receiver too.
takes.mechanism: He re-aggravated the hamstring before the season (a player they flag as having a real hamstring problem) and is coming back into the league's highest-pace passing offense.

takes.why: He is most likely returning this week, which caps the Raiders pass-catcher streamers behind him.
takes.mechanism: Clint Kubiak said Bowers will practice this week — though they openly distrust Kubiak's injury reporting ('he is an absolute liar').

takes.why: A juggernaut defense still available in most leagues — grab for a two-week run.
takes.mechanism: They are playing great defense and draw Tampa Bay and Miami back to back.

takes.why: Same profile as Minnesota — add now for the back-to-back window.
takes.mechanism: They are playing great defense and draw Miami and Las Vegas back to back.

takes.why: The specific Week 3 defensive stream, with a multi-week runway behind it.
takes.mechanism: They face Atlanta on Thursday night where Michael Pennix Jr. may be better than Cooper Rush but has no problem turning the ball over; then Baker Mayfield's Buccaneers, who have not been good, and then Micah Parsons comes off IR to boost the unit, possibly against a Caleb-less Chicago.

takes.why: A secondary streaming option this week.
takes.mechanism: They draw Tennessee, one of the offenses being actively targeted by streamers.

takes.why: Buy low immediately — before Thursday Night Football — on a TE5 rest-of-season who just gave you 3.5 PPR points.
takes.mechanism: His route participation roughly doubled from week 1 to week 2 (48% to 84%, or 94% by Kofler's data), meaning week 1 was an ACL testing ground and he is now a full go; the Packers gave him a 4-year, $75M extension (up to $92M, $27M signing-bonus guarantee) so they aren't worried about the knee; and with Jayden Reed hurt and no WR depth behind Watson/Golden he is the only reliable 5-to-12-yard option for Jordan Love, plus a beatable Falcons defense on TNF.

takes.why: Start him on Thursday night and expect the breakout to be coming.
takes.mechanism: His snap count jumped from 50-something percent to 98%, they paid him top-tier tight end money, last week's bad game came in rough weather, and with Jayden Reed out the Packers have no possession receiver at all — Watson and Golden are not going to catch 11 balls — so they have to start drawing up plays for Kraft to get the offense going.

takes.why: One of the most obvious buy-lows in fantasy — still a top-30 rest-of-season player (WR12, 26th overall) despite 5.8 and 10 PPR points.
takes.mechanism: His 23% target share is already higher than the 22% he had last year when he finished as a top-five fantasy WR; he caught six of eight targets while facing a safety over the top (Schottenheimer said the double teams on Pickens are what freed CeeDee Lamb for single coverage, and Prescott confirmed the attention), which is a two-week sample problem, not a role problem; and four of the next six matchups (Bucs, Packers, Cardinals) are pristine for the Dallas passing game.

takes.why: Worth buying low now and moving him up the board meaningfully — he should be valued over Quinshon Judkins.
takes.mechanism: With Rico Dowdle hurt he played 72% of the snaps and took over 50% of the rush attempts while running the majority of the routes and holding a 13% target share (roughly top-10 among RBs); that is the exact role Kenneth Gainwell turned into a top-five receiving RB season in this offense last year, and Dowdle's toe injury (possible turf toe, which lingers for RBs) removes the man blocking his early-down work.

takes.why: Trade for him now, before Thursday night — he is in store for an early breakout and belongs in the Jameson Williams / Terry McLaurin range, above Rome Odunze.
takes.mechanism: He and Christian Watson are mirror images through two weeks — both at a 27% target share, 12.6 vs 12.5 aDOT, 33% of air yards each, 40% of end-zone targets each — his week-2 line hides two drawn DPI/holding penalties downfield, and with Jayden Reed hurt plus Savion Williams on IR the only remaining competition is Bo Melton, a converted defensive back. Bad run blocking also forces this offense to throw.

takes.why: Start him on Thursday night.
takes.mechanism: Green Bay has been pass-heavy, and with Jayden Reed out the target tree narrows to Watson, Golden and Kraft.

takes.why: Still buying low and keeping him around his 42nd-overall rest-of-season rank despite a three-catch, 16-yard week.
takes.mechanism: He leads the team with an 18% target share (Godwin only 12%) with no Mike Evans and a diminished Godwin, and new OC Zac Robinson is deploying him exactly the way he used Drake London in Atlanta — heavy pre-snap motion (no WR had more motion at the snap in week 1) and slot alignments for free releases — so once Baker Mayfield and the line stabilize, the layup looks should convert to London-like production; the drag on him is quarterback play, not usage (worst catchable air yards in the league at 39%).

takes.why: He looks terrible to open the season and may already be hurt — the main downside risk attached to the Bucs' pass catchers.
takes.mechanism: Week 1's 82% completion rate was fake — all checkdowns with no touchdowns and Bucky Irving catching seven of 23 completions — then week 2 was 61% completions at 5.4 yards per attempt with an interception while being outplayed by Deshaun Watson, and he has been seen on the sideline getting his pec worked on again like last year.

takes.why: Buy low on a clear RB1 whose rest-of-season value is only rising from 41st overall — a third-round re-draft value in the Achane tier.
takes.mechanism: This is not a split backfield: 17 carries at 5.2 yards per carry to Kenny Gainwell's two, 77% of snaps, 54% of routes and 81% of rush attempts in week 2 (70% snaps and 69% rush attempts across two weeks), with Sean Tucker completely absent from the goal-line role — the same usage profile as the healthy end of his 2024 rookie year when he averaged 18.3 fantasy points per game.

takes.why: A hold-your-nose buy low — his owner may give him away for nothing after eight and 6.7 PPR points.
takes.mechanism: He is the clear alpha with Michael Pittman hurt — 19 targets for a 25% target share (top five in the NFL), third in the league in routes run at 88 (44 a week), on a team where Aaron Rodgers has the third-most pass attempts and will throw even more now that Rico Dowdle is hurt — the only thing broken is a two-week drops issue from a seven-year proven player, and five of the next six matchups (Browns, Colts, Bucs, Browns, Saints) are favorable.

takes.why: Buy low if you can after a bad week.
takes.mechanism: Nobody is coming for his job — over 80% of snaps last week, 76% of snaps and 71% of rush attempts through two weeks, even after the Chiefs cut Ademari/DeMarcato — and he is in a good offense that should feed him checkdown targets and red-zone carries; nobody expects efficiency from a 26-year-old with his injury history.

takes.why: Very worried about his actual physical ability — keep starting him for now but he becomes a buy-low candidate only in a week or two, and they would trade him straight up for Jeremiyah Love or Chuba Hubbard today.
takes.mechanism: He is averaging 2.96 yards per carry with 50% of his runs going for two or fewer yards and ranks 42nd of 43 RBs in first downs (two on 24 carries); the offensive line is dead last in yards before contact with Pro Bowler Tyler Smith on IR until week 5, and this is a back who takes exactly what is blocked and creates nothing — plus on tape he looks slow, 'like he is carrying extra pounds.' The next two matchups (Ravens, Texans) are difficult.

takes.why: Quietly buy low from a possibly 0-2 owner who spent a fourth or fifth rounder on him.
takes.mechanism: His former girlfriend's attorneys filed a motion to permanently seal the evidence and discovery in the criminal case, which reads like a settlement, so a return date should be coming; and the Packers' replacement backfield (Chris Brooks, Kaleb Johnson, Marshawn Lloyd) has been so bad that he walks straight back into 15-plus touches a game.

takes.why: Buy in — put chips into this; Andy has him as a QB10 from week 3 through 17 (one host said QB20) and they would start him this week over both Tyler Shough and Joe Burrow.
takes.mechanism: The change is philosophical, not just hot passing: Carolina is playing the fastest pace in the NFL at 23 seconds per play and is number one in neutral pass rate, which is the opposite of the Chuba/Rico run-team identity, so either he throws well or he fails and has to throw more — and with a bad Carolina defense this is the same 'must throw all game' storm that made the 2025 Bengals and Cowboys fantasy goldmines. Supporting: QB2 in fantasy, three TDs in each of the last two weeks with one INT, 8.9 yards per attempt and a 10.5 aDOT, both blowing away his career averages, plus Waller as a red-zone option and a healthy Jalen Coker.

takes.why: He is back for fantasy — Jason has him as high as QB5 rest of season, Andy at QB8-9 (he finished QB11 each of the last two years), and everyone would rather have him than Bryce Young every week.
takes.mechanism: Matt Nagy is gone and the goal-line creativity is back (tap passes, rollout play-action with three options open), plus the addition of Kenneth Walker forces defenses to honor play-action and keep bodies at the line of scrimmage — it is not about any individual target, since Rashee Rice, Worthy and Thornton have not been individually productive; and Mahomes' own rushing will only grow as he trusts the leg, which adds free touchdowns.

takes.why: A start of the week — 100% in every lineup on Thursday night, and people will wrongly be afraid to play him.
takes.mechanism: In the games he played with Michael Penix last year he was on pace for 180 targets and finished as the WR1 on a week / WR5 overall, so there is direct evidence that Penix consolidates targets to the stars even in bad conditions; this is Penix's first week back with a non-Cooper Rush situation.

takes.why: Play Bijan and log out.
takes.mechanism: With Penix last year he was on pace for over 100 targets, and even with Atlanta running zero red-zone plays in two games he still catches a pile of checkdowns — the floor is volume, not scheme health.

takes.why: Not moving away from him entirely and he is startable over Loveland, but they would not dial up a big game from him Thursday.
takes.mechanism: It is a first start at Lambeau on Thursday night for a quarterback coming off injury, and like London we simply haven't been able to see what the offense can do.

takes.why: Bench him — you should be willing to go into the waiver dumpster and start a Dalton Schultz type over him even though it hurts.
takes.mechanism: He has one catch and is now looking at a third-string quarterback: Tyson Bagent is in the concussion protocol after self-reporting post-game (hard to clear in a short week) behind an already-injured Caleb Williams, leaving Bagent or Case Keenum against the Eagles.

takes.why: Bench all Bears pass catchers this week.
takes.mechanism: Chicago is down to the backup of the backup at quarterback (Bagent in concussion protocol, Caleb Williams hurt) against the Eagles, and nothing about this offense has produced a normal, projectable game yet.

takes.why: Stay in the flames — start Shough over Joe Burrow this week (but Bryce Young over Shough), while conceding Burrow is the better rest-of-season asset.
takes.mechanism: He leads the league in passing volume, he is at home, and the matchup comparison favors him: Burrow has to go into Pittsburgh, one of the best defenses in the league so far, in a dirty AFC North game (last time in Pittsburgh Burrow finished QB18 with one touchdown). The caveat they raise against him is Calvin Banks out plus Max Crosby, and the Raiders currently rank as the number one fantasy defense.

takes.why: A one-week matchup sit behind both Bryce Young and Tyler Shough — not a rest-of-season downgrade.
takes.mechanism: He plays at Pittsburgh, which has been one of the best defenses in the league through two weeks, in an AFC North game with a modest 42.5 total; absent matchups they would just stick with Burrow.

takes.why: A good add, worth paying up for in dynasty or if you have a quarterback bye-week problem — but a tempered version of old Jameis.
takes.mechanism: Jackson Dart is out for the season, and while Harbaugh's philosophy will not permit the turnover-for-touchdown Winston experience and the team wants to run and play defense, they will eventually have to throw — so expect 300 yards and two touchdowns with two picks, not a nerfed backup. Week 1's dud was mostly the Rams' defense plus a banged-up Malik Nabers.

takes.why: Also a reasonable dynasty/bye-week add behind Winston.
takes.mechanism: Dart's season-ending knee surgery opens the entire Giants quarterback room.

takes.why: Easy Jeremiyah Love over Javonte Williams for the rest of the season — actively offer Javonte for him in any league even expecting a no.
takes.mechanism: Talent over opportunity: rookie running backs get more and more work as the season goes on, and that is doubly true for a number-three overall pick, plus he may still be shaking off the ankle — whereas Javonte's ceiling is capped by his own ability.

takes.why: Yes, trade for Hubbard — Jason would even send Javonte Williams for him straight up (Andy wouldn't have the guts).
takes.mechanism: He is going to catch the football in an offense that is now playing the fastest pace in the NFL and throwing at the highest neutral rate, and Jonathan Brooks is out on IR after core-muscle surgery.

takes.why: Jason takes Henderson over Chuba Hubbard for the rest of the season, definitively.
takes.mechanism: He can whiff on a bunch of pass plays and run for two yards a carry on 80% of his carries and still have a fine fantasy season because he is going to break long ones.

takes.why: Expect him to get more run and hope he becomes the guy — but do not start any Packers running back on Thursday night.
takes.mechanism: On tape he is the only Green Bay back who looks like an explosive athlete (all three hosts independently noticed his first touch); Chris Brooks leads snaps only because they trust him in pass protection and went 4 for 11 last game, and Marshawn Lloyd lost a fumble.

takes.why: Do not start him — he has not been good.
takes.mechanism: He leads the Packers' backfield in snaps only because they trust him in pass-blocking situations, and he went 4 carries for 11 yards last game inside a mixture that has produced offensive inefficiency.

takes.why: Not afraid to start defenses against the Chargers right now — the offense may bounce forward but probably not enough, starting in Buffalo.
takes.mechanism: The Chargers are 30th in EPA per play, 30th in percentage of drives resulting in a score and 31st in turnover differential, have another offensive line injury, and lost Ladd McConkie — the plays with Ladd in looked fine, without him they could not do anything; the drops have been nasty and turned into interceptions. The hosts explicitly do not blame McDaniel or Herbert for the drops.

takes.why: Slightly more worried about him after this week's roster move.
takes.mechanism: The 49ers signed Brandon Cooks to the practice squad and he could be moved up soon given their injuries — the add conversation started in the context of losing Robinson, with Christian Kirk still too many weeks away.

takes.why: Bench all Bears pass catchers this week.
takes.mechanism: Same quarterback collapse — Bagent in the concussion protocol behind an injured Caleb Williams, Case Keenum the alternative, versus the Eagles.

takes.why: Sell him now as his 30th-ranked rest-of-season player — he would not be drafted until the late third or early fourth round today.
takes.mechanism: 20 carries for 74 yards (3.7 YPC) because Miami has no pass-catching threat (Malik Washington a slot merchant, Caleb Douglas hurt, two other rookies, an unproven TE), so defenses load the box on 36% of his carries, the third-highest rate in the NFL; Malik Willis also steals goal-line work and the Dolphins are averaging the fewest fantasy-relevant plays per game in the database era.

takes.why: Still the only startable Dolphin — play him even in a terrible offense against Kansas City.
takes.mechanism: Volume floor holds even in the worst games (24 carries for 74 and 3 catches for 19 in Week 2); no touchdown yet, which they flag as the real risk.

takes.why: The biggest sell-high in fantasy — trade him one-for-one for essentially anyone, he is only the 93rd-ranked rest-of-season player.
takes.mechanism: About to turn 32, 23 carries for 105 yards produced only 10.5 fantasy points with no receiving role; O'Connell called him sore afterwards, DeeJay Dallas was signed midweek and will take work, and Jordan Mason returns from IR in roughly three weeks, so the flex value lasts two to three weeks.

takes.why: Sell into the Week 2 breakout — he is only the 61st-ranked rest-of-season player and the market paid a fifth-round pick for him.
takes.mechanism: His 60% snap share and 67% rush share were manufactured by Rhamondre Stevenson's early fumble (18 fumbles since 2021, most in the NFL) rather than earned, he averaged 2.7 YPC excluding a 39-yard touchdown run, and with A.J. Brown out defenses stack the box against a Patriots offense with no explosive pass-catchers.

takes.why: Sell high on every Carolina skill player including Hubbard — nobody thinks he is a 20-point-per-game back.
takes.mechanism: RB8 at 17.8-19.1 fantasy points per game on 66% of snaps, but the production came against the Bears (a possibly historically bad defense) and a Falcons team with no pass rush; his only prior top-12 finish back-doored in on receiving work.

takes.why: A must-start this week against Cleveland — one of only five running backs to finish top-12 in both weeks.
takes.mechanism: Jonathon Brooks went to IR, A.J. Dillon is not good and Carolina did not sign Austin Ekeler, so the backfield is fully his; they add that they would rather have drafted him than Quinshon Judkins.

takes.why: Sell into the 100-yard game — the Carolina passing explosion is schedule-driven and his catch rate will cap the big days.
takes.mechanism: 27% target share and 88 yards per game on only a 59% catch rate, produced against the Bears and a Falcons defense that blitzes heavily without generating pressure.

takes.why: Flip him one-for-one for Matthew Golden right now — Golden is the better talent in the more stable offense.
takes.mechanism: Team-leading 29% target share and 102 yards per game off a two-game sample against soft pass defenses; undrafted free agent whose perceived value is inflated by Bryce Young's start.

takes.why: The whole Carolina offense is fool's gold and Young is the centerpiece of the fraud — sell now, he will eat his words in a month if wrong.
takes.mechanism: Tied for the NFL lead with 6 passing touchdowns on 73 attempts (6th-most, inflated by trailing big in Week 1) and 9.8 yards per attempt against a 6.3 YPA baseline over his last two seasons — a mark that would rival the best ever; the new play-caller (Brad Idzik over Dave Canales) is a real but smaller effect.

takes.why: Start him over Justin Herbert, Drake Maye and Matthew Stafford this week — they moved him up to QB14, one spot ahead of Herbert, live on the episode.
takes.mechanism: Three-touchdown games in back-to-back weeks, Cleveland is 22nd in fantasy points allowed to QBs and Myles Garrett is gone, so the matchup is not a deterrent; Jason backed it with a $100 bet against Herbert.

takes.why: Perfect sell-high on a soon-to-be-33-year-old — trade him one-for-one for Josh Downs or Jaylen Warren while he looks like a top-10 WR.
takes.mechanism: 24% target share and a team-best 31% targets per route run on only 60% route participation (16.5 ppg, 7.5 targets), but Jayden Daniels is out (four to six weeks with a brace if no surgery, season over if there is), and Washington is deliberately getting Terry McLaurin more involved.

takes.why: Bench him this week — they will not play any Washington pass-catcher.
takes.mechanism: Backup quarterback (Marcus Mariota) against the Seahawks with Washington implied for 16.8 points, the lowest team total on the slate.

takes.why: Buy the rest-of-season profile even with Daniels out, but bench him this week — the matchup is brutal.
takes.mechanism: Worst catchable-target rate in the NFL at 54%, and Marcus Mariota historically feeds him: 3.53 yards per route run and 14.3 fantasy points per game across five Mariota starts last year, a WR14 pace; he also had a touchdown and a long catch wiped out by penalties in Week 2.

takes.why: Cash in immediately — he is a top-15 fantasy WR right now and not even a top-115 player rest of season.
takes.mechanism: Both weeks were carried by long touchdowns (46 yards, then a 55-yarder after three missed Bucs tackles); his 22% target share is barely ahead of KC Concepcion's 20% with Harold Fannin also involved, so he profiles as a boom-bust receiver who scores under 10 points without a 30-plus-yard play, and Shedeur Sanders taking over would cut the downfield throws.

takes.why: The only Cleveland pass-catcher they would play this week, but below Adonai Mitchell on their board.
takes.mechanism: He will get the targets and the high-value (downfield, red-zone) targets in a game Carolina is favored in; they will not touch the rest of the Browns' skill players.

takes.why: He is the better rest-of-season Browns receiver — trade Boston for him straight up if you can.
takes.mechanism: First-round pick with a 20% target share who is the more polished route runner and will work the slot, which is where Shedeur Sanders will be most comfortable throwing when he takes over.

takes.why: Absolutely cooked — sell him for Emeka Egbuka, a banged-up DJ Moore or Jameson Williams while anyone still bids.
takes.mechanism: Dead last in targets per route run and separation among WRs with 10-plus targets (per Scott Barrett's chart), below even Chris Godwin, Cooper Kupp and Dyami Brown; he cost a third-round pick and would now be a fifth-round pick.

takes.why: Start him this week despite the usage — if not here, then never.
takes.mechanism: Targeted on only 11% of routes, but Kansas City is a 10.5-point road favorite with a 28.5-point implied total, the second-highest of the season so far.

takes.why: Not panic-selling, but actively shopping him — he has fallen from near a first-round asset to his 32nd-ranked rest-of-season player, and any of George Pickens, Drake London, Parker Washington, DeVonta Smith or Tee Higgins one-for-one is a win.
takes.mechanism: Re-dislocated shoulder (fully participated Wednesday with clean X-rays, which is why he is not a panic sell) plus Jaxson Dart lost for the season; Jameis Winston is a materially less efficient offense even if not a disaster.

takes.why: No longer a guaranteed start — benching him is defensible, though they would still play him over the Boston/Adonai Mitchell/Bateman tier.
takes.mechanism: Shoulder popped out of the socket last week and he was barely targeted afterwards, in a 38.5-total game with 68% chance of rain and high winds and Jameis Winston (11 of 27 last week) at quarterback.

takes.why: The single best buy in the video — borderline top-50 rest of season, a fifth-round pick if redrafting, and levels above A.J. Brown; he has the best individual matchup on the entire Thursday slate.
takes.mechanism: Tied for the team-high 27% target share with no Jayden Reed; his Week 2 line hides two drawn personal fouls; with A.J. Terrell out he sees mostly Mike Hughes, 89th of 128 in coverage at 1.4 yards allowed per coverage snap.

takes.why: Keep and start both Packers receivers — he is Sal's WR10 on the week.
takes.mechanism: Tied with Golden for a team-high 27% target share with a good quarterback and an above-average play-caller; both should see six to twelve targets weekly.

takes.why: Sell him for anyone ranked above him — Luther Burden III, Chuba Hubbard, Emeka Egbuka, Colston Loveland, Jaylen Warren, DJ Moore, Bucky Irving or Jameson Williams all qualify.
takes.mechanism: Six to eight weeks out with a high ankle sprain that nearly required surgery, and a 230-pound receiver will not beat that timeline; add a ramp-up period on top.

takes.why: A clear buy and about to be his 65th-ranked rest-of-season player — take him over A.J. Brown easily and trade Aaron Jones or Stefon Diggs for him.
takes.mechanism: He is the Colts' full-time No. 1 with Alec Pierce out at least six weeks; the market still prices him as a slot complement, so you cannot get a fair running back back for him.

takes.why: Mike's start of the week against Houston — he is the Colts' number one receiver, full stop.
takes.mechanism: Nine targets for 7-72 last week, 30% first-read target share and 29% of the team's receiving yards with Alec Pierce out of the picture; Houston is bleeding points to WRs and Downs averages over 10 fantasy points in five career games versus them.

takes.why: Andy's tight end start of the week — he would be shocked if Kelce doesn't score.
takes.mechanism: Leads all NFL pass catchers in yards after the catch and leads the Chiefs in targets per route run; Kansas City are 11.5-point road favorites in Miami, and the eye test says he is in better shape than last year.

takes.why: His TE2 on the week and one of the best tight ends to own in fantasy right now — start him over Tucker Kraft.
takes.mechanism: Leads the Chiefs with a 25% target share and leads the NFL in yards after the catch; he is separating and creating space, and Kansas City's short-to-intermediate play-action offense fits him because Rice looks bad and Worthy is inconsistent — though a 36-year-old will not sustain 100-yard touchdown games.

takes.why: One of the best buy-lows in all of fantasy and his Thursday flex play over Denzel Boston and Colston Loveland.
takes.mechanism: Ran 84% of routes in Week 2 after about 40% in Week 1, so targets follow; with Jayden Reed gone he is the only Packer you trust on third-and-seven over the middle, and the offensive-lineman chatter is dismissed because Green Bay signed a blocking tight end for that.

takes.why: Mike's tight end start of the week for Thursday night ('Tucker 2x4'), acquired via a second- and fourth-round trade.
takes.mechanism: Played 98% of snaps — a huge jump back to full-time — and with Jayden Reed out he should dominate the middle of the field; Atlanta is 29th in schedule-adjusted points allowed to tight ends and already got beaten up by Pat Freiermuth and Darren Waller.

takes.why: Probably the best buy-low in all of fantasy football — he is his 23rd-ranked rest-of-season player, so sell Nabers for him instantly.
takes.mechanism: Rest-of-season ranking is essentially unchanged while the market has cooled on a slow start; league-mates who aren't paying attention will let him go at a discount.

takes.why: A top-25 rest-of-season player — take him over Jaylen Waddle or Malik Nabers one-for-one, and trade Chuba Hubbard for him.
takes.mechanism: His rest-of-season rankings have him unbelievably high for a player still being treated as a waiver-tier name.

takes.why: Red-alert time — he is projected out this week and Sal would trade him for Breece Hall plus DeVonta Smith, though he will not sell truly low.
takes.mechanism: Second straight missed week, not practicing at all, and McVay said on the radio he is not getting better; he has all the symptoms of a core-muscle injury without the diagnosis, and if surgery follows it is six-plus additional weeks.

takes.why: He is not playing this week and they do not know how quickly he returns.
takes.mechanism: Did not practice Wednesday; McVay volunteered that it is not a hernia and not an ACL but that Nacua 'is not making great progress' — naming the injuries a player doesn't have is itself a bad sign, and a groin issue can take multiple weeks.

takes.why: His WR4 of the week — start him over Ja'Marr Chase, Justin Jefferson, Chris Olave, DeVonta Smith and Garrett Wilson.
takes.mechanism: Nearly 34 years old and still playing on the best offense in the NFL with Nacua out, coming off a big Monday night; the projection, not the name, drives the rank.

takes.why: Projected for literally 0.0 points this week — start Matthew Golden over him without hesitation; he is still a buy rest of season (trade Achane for him instantly).
takes.mechanism: Has not practiced two days running with a hamstring, is traveling to Brazil for a game on a surface that wrecked footing last time, and even if active he would rank only around WR25 given usage limits.

takes.why: A fine one-week streamer if Flowers sits, but he will have zero trade value even after a good game.
takes.mechanism: His entire role exists because Zay Flowers is out; anyone paying attention knows he reverts to a waiver player the Wednesday Flowers is healthy.

takes.why: A top-three tight end this week if Zay Flowers is out; if Flowers plays, start Dalton Schultz instead.
takes.mechanism: He is Baltimore's number one red-zone option and the 1A/1B in the offense without Flowers; Schultz's TE7 projection came off a 14-target career game that won't repeat.

takes.why: His TE7 at 12.2 projected points and the right flex over Terry McLaurin or Stefon Diggs — but he is 'a very bad tight end' long term.
takes.mechanism: Nico Collins out consolidates the target share, and Indianapolis is the tight-end funnel Kelce just obliterated; his 12-for-140 last week came on 14 targets and a lot of garbage time.

takes.why: Jason's tight end start of the week — 'such a good play right now'.
takes.mechanism: 12 catches on 14 targets for 140 yards versus Cincinnati including long broken-field runs, and the Colts are the defense you target; with Nico Collins not practicing, Houston's offense is consolidated to Schultz and Montgomery.

takes.why: Andy's start of the week for a second straight week against Arizona.
takes.mechanism: Leads all quarterbacks in EPA per play as an 8.5-point home favorite; he is at an 8.9% touchdown rate with room to regress to his normal 7% and still be excellent, and it doesn't matter that Stribling, Demarcus Robinson, Christian Kirk and maybe Mike Evans are unavailable.

takes.why: Start him this week over Tyler Shough, but trade him — he is only the 68th-ranked player rest of season and a sixth- or seventh-round quarterback if you redrafted.
takes.mechanism: Quarterbacks never rank highly on his one-list valuation outside Josh Allen, so two great weeks are a selling opportunity: flip Purdy for Matthew Golden or D'Andre Swift and stream quarterback off waivers (Jordan Love, Kyler Murray).

takes.why: Jason's start of the week at home against the Jets.
takes.mechanism: 327 yards and four touchdowns last week; he has averaged 21 fantasy points per game at home in a dome since 2022, and Detroit has the fifth-highest implied team total of the week.

takes.why: Mike's stream of the week and the quarterback he is rolling out in a big week.
takes.mechanism: First player in NFL history with 3,000 passing yards and a 67% completion rate through his first 13 career games; Kellen Moore's pace gives him roughly five extra drop-backs, an extra drive per game, and the offensive line gets a boost if Achane's Miami counterpart matters less than expected.

takes.why: Andy's running back start of the week coming off a dud — 'these are the kind of starts you need sometimes'.
takes.mechanism: Only eight opportunities and under five fantasy points last week but he still out-snapped Woody Marks; Indianapolis is 30th in EPA per rush attempt and 31st in yards per carry allowed.

takes.why: Jason's start of the week and a solid RB2 at home against Tennessee.
takes.mechanism: 16 and 18 opportunities in two weeks as the clear lead back; with Jaxson Dart gone the Giants will lean on the run and play defense, and Jameis Winston should check down to him more.

takes.why: Very playable this week even as the backup — Mike's start of the week against Denver.
takes.mechanism: Six yards per carry on 22 attempts, second only to Kenneth Walker among backs; Denver is dead last in EPA per rush and in yards after contact per attempt allowed and 29th in fantasy points allowed to RBs.

takes.why: Start him as the stack with Purdy against Arizona — he is the last man standing.
takes.mechanism: Lining up 50% out wide, 45% in the slot and 5% in the backfield, and with Kittle limited coming back Shanahan is out of other options in his 'this is how we win' script.

takes.why: Could not imagine benching him — he expects a billion points in the Buffalo game and a very fine fantasy week.
takes.mechanism: He barely practiced last week and was a decoy on under half the snaps, but is a full participant Wednesday; Buffalo is 31st in points per drive allowed, 28th in pass success rate allowed and 30th in fantasy points allowed to WRs, leaking specifically to slot receivers, and the Chargers desperately need him.

takes.why: Start him slightly over Matthew Golden, Ladd McConkey and Malik Nabers as a Nacua replacement — but he is behind Parker Washington as an asset.
takes.mechanism: He is healthier than McConkey, who may still be wearing a protective vest for a chest/rib injury.

takes.why: Start him — he looks like Buffalo's number one receiver even with DJ Moore on the field.
takes.mechanism: Always been excellent per route; now healthy after playing about 38% of snaps through a knee injury last year, he is finally running a full route load as the 25th overall pick.

takes.why: Trade DK Metcalf straight up for him and trade Josh Jacobs for him immediately.
takes.mechanism: In a tight-end premium format he is close to Tee Higgins as a top-50 rest-of-season asset.

takes.why: Start him over Harold Fannin, Kenyon Sadiq and Oronde Gadsden II, and roster him for the rest of the season — but behind Schultz, Terrance Ferguson and Jake Ferguson.
takes.mechanism: As good a touchdown bet as any tight end because he is enormous and always involved near the red zone; his snap counts are very low now and should rise as the season goes on.

takes.why: Not good enough to start — they take Waller over him even in the same game.
takes.mechanism: 17% target share through two weeks in a three-way Browns split with Boston and Concepcion.

takes.why: Dust — trade him straight up for Travis Kelce or Mark Andrews if anyone will do it.
takes.mechanism: Buried in a spread-out Browns target tree; the one upside path is Shedeur Sanders taking over and throwing shorter, quicker passes.

takes.why: Start him over Darren Waller — the touchdown odds are lower but the snaps are not.
takes.mechanism: Two touchdowns last week, he is on the field more than Waller and used between the twenties, and both can catch touchdowns; snaps break the tie.

takes.why: A secondary start of the week and a waiver add if Puka Nacua is out.
takes.mechanism: With Nacua inactive the Rams' targets redistribute to him; they rank him ahead of Waller, Sadiq and Gadsden this week.

takes.why: A bench stash and DFS play with a genuine breakout path this week, not a start over Waller or Ferguson.
takes.mechanism: Mason Taylor did not practice and looks out; Sadiq is a first-round pick with an off-the-charts athletic profile, and athletic testing matters at tight end more than at any other position — a first-rounder who produces while the starter is out simply takes the job.

takes.why: The moment to buy low is now — he should have a much better rest of season.
takes.mechanism: With Alec Pierce missing an extended period he benefits from target consolidation; he was a yards-after-catch machine in college and led all pass catchers in YAC through the first three weeks last season, and his YAC per catch has collapsed from 10.8 to 3.8, so the touchdowns are propping up tiny yardage totals.

takes.why: Start Pitts over Oronde Gadsden II — the projections are a wash (8.0 vs 8.2) so take the guy you know will be on the field.
takes.mechanism: Pitts runs routes tonight with Michael Penix and has upside; the Chargers signed Charlie Kolar and traded for David Njoku precisely because they don't trust Gadsden to block, so McDaniel can pull him in hurry-up situations.

takes.why: An okay desperation start — the injuries force him onto the field almost every play.
takes.mechanism: Njoku and Kolar are on IR, so he plays by default; he is not a complete tight end (athletic, free-releasing, non-blocker) and had a touchdown on only two targets last week.

takes.why: Mike starts him the moment he is active; Jason remains skeptical until he sees him play.
takes.mechanism: Limited participant Wednesday and again Thursday after missing time — practice trend is positive but the active designation is the gate.

takes.why: Start Brock Bowers over him and sell high on Kittle while you still can.
takes.mechanism: Coming off a big week while still recovering, and San Francisco cannot overload him — Deebo is the designed focal point this week.

takes.why: Start him — he was a start-of-the-week finalist and if he fails in this matchup there is no week you can play him.
takes.mechanism: Carolina is dead last in yards per carry allowed, rushing touchdowns allowed and EPA per rush this year, was bad last year and was one of the worst run defenses of all time the year before — a true run funnel; Cleveland are only two-point underdogs so the touchdown equity is there.

takes.why: Should be okay and playable if healthy — Mike would even start him over Judkins.
takes.mechanism: Running for 4.7 yards a carry and the Giants cannot stop running backs; volume went 7 carries in Week 1 to 14 in Week 2, but he and Tyjae Spears both missed Wednesday with ankles.

takes.why: A bench week — the talent is real but the environment is not.
takes.mechanism: A 24% target share that is 'the biggest slice of a turd pie' — Tennessee will not throw, he has not seen a single target 20-plus yards downfield all year, and the game has bad weather and the lowest over/under of the week (38.5).

takes.why: Playable this week — Mike would start him over DK Metcalf and over Denzel Boston.
takes.mechanism: He is ahead of Garrett Wilson in target share and the Detroit game environment (over has hit in six straight Lions games, 47.5 total) is far better than the Pittsburgh game.

takes.why: Keep starting him — volatility is the price of admission for a WR3/flex who wins you weeks.
takes.mechanism: Played 97% of snaps; a waiver receiver who reliably gives you seven to nine points cannot win a matchup, and Williams was drafted to go nuclear.

takes.why: A perfect buy-low — the right return when selling Rashee Rice or A.J. Brown.
takes.mechanism: Ranked above both of them on his rest-of-season list while the market treats him as a volatile flex.

takes.why: Andy would go back to the well this week; Mike would rather play Adonai Mitchell and avoid him.
takes.mechanism: The targets are there, but the Steelers offense is hard to watch and Cincinnati is a tough spot in a 42.5-total AFC North game.

takes.why: A floor-plus-touchdown play you could do worse than.
takes.mechanism: Cincinnati has been the tight-end funnel to attack for roughly eight straight years, and nobody else in Pittsburgh's passing game is a credible touchdown-scorer.

takes.why: Take the volume if he is alone in the backfield, but he is definitely still injured.
takes.mechanism: Back at practice but limited, while Rico Dowdle still has not practiced — a Warren-only backfield is the bull case.

takes.why: Worth half your FAAB in a standard 12-teamer — probably a discount — and a fair one-for-one return for Aaron Jones or Stefon Diggs.
takes.mechanism: His start-sit tool projects Warren at 14.7 points versus Aaron Jones at 12.7 for Week 3, pending whether Rico Dowdle plays.

takes.why: He wants one week where Warren and Dowdle are both out and the late-round rookie gets the full role.
takes.mechanism: An outrageously good college analytical profile and a jack-of-all-trades skill set; as good a receiver as he is a runner, a perfect Aaron Rodgers checkdown target the way Kenny Gainwell was last year.

takes.why: Andy's almost-upset pick is the Steelers, and the playable fantasy asset in that game is the defense.
takes.mechanism: Through two weeks Pittsburgh is first against quarterbacks, second against wide receivers and fifth against tight ends and will bring the pass rush — with the caveat that the two samples were Cooper Rush and a struggling Drake Maye; Jalen Ramsey's status is the swing factor.

takes.why: An easy start along with Higgins, Burrow and Chase Brown, but do not expect prolific numbers in Pittsburgh.
takes.mechanism: Cincinnati's offense has not clicked on all cylinders yet (the defense has carried them) and the Steelers' DNA is pass defense; low 42.5 total.

takes.why: No reason to trade a borderline top-five rest-of-season player just because you have injuries elsewhere.
takes.mechanism: He is roughly fifth overall on the rest-of-season list; two weeks is not a reason to move a cornerstone.

takes.why: Mike would start him over Jadarian Price, but the game environment is unexciting.
takes.mechanism: Seattle salted away the fourth quarter with Wilson after Price was hurt, and Washington was very bad against RBs last year; Seattle's 24-point implied total is fine but the game should disappear fast on few plays.

takes.why: Good news that he was seen in practice — he is in a good spot as a seven-point favorite.
takes.mechanism: Through three quarters last week Price had the carry lead; the fourth-quarter Wilson workload came after Price was knocked out.

takes.why: A sneaky start in a blowout spot — he could get ten carries in the fourth quarter alone.
takes.mechanism: The rookie has looked great behind Kenneth Walker and Kansas City is a 10.5-point road favorite with a 28.5-point implied total against Miami, so the fourth quarter is his.

takes.why: Stash him (and Kaelon Black) ahead of a better weekly projection like R.J. Harvey — the home-run outcome is what you are buying.
takes.mechanism: If Kenneth Walker or Christian McCaffrey gets hurt, the handcuff inherits a league-winning role; a bench player you won't start should be bought for contingency, not projection.

takes.why: A stash worth a bench spot over a startable-but-capped option.
takes.mechanism: Direct contingency on Christian McCaffrey's workload; contingent upside beats a flex projection for a bench slot.

takes.why: The number-one waiver pickup in about half of leagues did not practice — they withdrew a Denver-backfield claim over it.
takes.mechanism: Official Wednesday report has Coleman as did-not-participate while J.K. Dobbins and R.J. Harvey were limited, so the two players he was supposed to replace practiced more than he did.

takes.why: Avoid the entire Denver backfield right now.
takes.mechanism: Coleman looked like the clear add early in the week but is not practicing with an ankle injury, while Dobbins and Harvey are both practicing on hamstrings — a three-way gross split.

takes.why: If Aaron Jones is out, Mike would start Claiborne over DeeJay Dallas for the explosive upside even though Dallas likely plays more.
takes.mechanism: Great speed and a good system fit; Andy counters that the team does not trust him and Dallas is the more trusted, higher-snap player.

takes.why: The more trusted Minnesota back who will play more snaps if Aaron Jones sits.
takes.mechanism: Signed midweek to the active roster and already ahead of the rookie in the coaching staff's trust hierarchy; Andy expects him to get more work regardless.

takes.why: His 31st-ranked rest-of-season player and a top-25 asset — buy him off the down week, and anyone trading Achane, Tuten or Tee Higgins for him is losing the deal.
takes.mechanism: Ranked far above both Achane (30th is not the same tier once you account for redraft cost) and Bhayshul Tuten (barely top-50); the Caleb Williams absence is a fair concern but priced in.

takes.why: Anyone who traded D'Andre Swift for Tuten fumbled the bag — he is barely a top-50 rest-of-season player.
takes.mechanism: Swift is a top-25 rest-of-season asset; the backfield-share argument for Tuten does not close a gap that large.

takes.why: Flex him slightly over D'Andre Swift this week; as an asset he is only around the 30th-ranked player.
takes.mechanism: Swift faces the Eagles' defensive line on Monday night without Caleb Williams and possibly with a third-string quarterback, in a game both teams may want to grind out.

takes.why: A nothing burger in any trade — do not pay for him, and trade him for Dalton Kincaid immediately if you own him.

strategy_notes.note: Off-field/suspension risk to an incumbent is a legitimate accelerant for a rookie's snap timeline [FF]: the day-2/day-3 rookie WR base rate (slow starts, second-half relevance) can be overridden when the player ahead of him is under league investigation or otherwise unlikely to be part of the team's future — the org starts developing the rookie sooner. Check the incumbent's status, not just the rookie's draft capital.

Sanctioned buy conditions for a 30+ receiver [Sal]: he normally avoids aging WRs, but names the exact conjunction that overrides it — (a) the target competition in the room has been vacated, (b) a real QB upgrade arrived, and (c) the ADP has already fallen for the age/injury narrative. All three must hold (A.J. Brown, McLaurin, Evans); efficiency stats that survived the down year (YPRR, first downs per route run, zero drops) are the confirmation that the skills, not the situation, are intact.

Four to six games is the read-the-team threshold [FF]: the hosts converge on refusing to judge a team before week 4 and making the call by weeks 4-6 — early enough to still act before the fantasy playoffs, late enough that schedule strength has evened out. They validate the rule against prior-year week-4 standings (Baltimore 1-3, Arizona 2-2 and never winning again) rather than asserting it.

Price an injury backup against the real starter tiers, not the hype [FF]: when a starter goes down and his backup's ADP spikes, ask where the backup would rank if you KNEW he was starting — put him next to the actual committee starters (Tuten, Price, Warren, Stevenson) and see whether you would take him over any of them. That anchor exposed a pick-37 ADP on a day-3 back with no college production on a low-scoring offense. Pair it with the combine-vs-production check (an A.J. Dillon profile: elite athletic testing that never produced in college).

Do not double- and triple-count a risk that is already in the price [Sal]: for aging or injury-prone veterans, age, injury history and a current camp tightness report are often the same risk restated three ways. Once the ADP has fallen to reflect the known profile, an additional narrative ('everybody on that team gets hurt') is not new information and should not produce a further discount. The test is whether the report changes the week-1 availability branch — 25 days to heal with 'not considered serious' does not.

Stale-ADP trap on news-flip players [FF]: an ADP formed during a player's bad-news window (Nabers' ACL recovery pessimism) is already obsolete the moment the news flips, and every manager in the room is staring at that same number hoping for the steal. Never plan a build around the printed ADP of a player whose situation just improved — assume he goes a full round or more earlier than the number says.

Price a stack by naming the players you pass on [FF]: before drafting a stack partner, pull the platform ADP for that exact pick and say out loud who else is on the board. If the opportunity cost is real (DJ Moore in the late fifth costs Jameson Williams / Luther Burden / Tuten / Price), do not force the stack — either wait for a later round where he is free or switch to a cheaper correlated piece (the late-round TE version of the same stack).

Camp reception counts by quarterback as a target-pecking-order proxy [FF]: they explicitly want, for every team, the full ordered list of how many catches each pass catcher made from the starting QB across training camp — and treat that ordering as real signal while dismissing preseason completion percentage as noise ('they should be failing in preseason'). It is a usage metric available before any snap chart exists, and it resolved their New England pecking order (Brown > Doubs > Stevenson > Douglas > Henry > Boutte).

Three-outcome (wild-card) classification and its roster cap [FF]: sort picks into 'guaranteed to produce on some level' vs wild cards whose range genuinely spans worthless / flex-worthy / league-winning, and deliberately carry only one or two wild cards on a roster — 'you really don't want a bunch of those'. The classification is also a filter for hype: a player who cannot plausibly reach the league-winning end (Bucky Irving with the pass-catching role gone, R.J. Harvey behind two names) does not belong in the bucket regardless of how exciting he is.
Anchor with elite RBs: two RBs in your first three picks (reliability, not breakout swings) — RBs fly early this year and the position is barren by round 5.

The RB dead zone is back — RB24 now costs a 5th-round pick (a 7th in 2024) — grab two elite backs in the first 3-4 rounds and refuse to pay for middling RB2/3s (Etienne, Montgomery, Warren, Pollard all priced above projection).
Elite QB prices are the cheapest in years — Lamar a full round-plus cheaper than last year's QB2; Burrow (rd 5) / Daniels and Hurts (rd 6) are legitimate value even for late-round-QB drafters.
Wait on QB in 1QB: Allen is the lone QB priced in round 2 while Daniels/Hurts/Maye deliver comparable upside ~50 picks later; rounds 10-11 are the last window for Kyler/Mahomes/Purdy types.
Avoid RBs on bad teams: backs on sub-7-win teams hit ADP only ~30% of the time; 2026 teams that are underdogs in 3+ of their first 4 (ARI, CLE, IND, LV, MIA, NYJ, DEN) create uphill starts.
Don't stash day-2/3 rookie WRs early (48%/30% snaps, 2-4 targets through week 6) — only first-round rookies start day one; spend late picks on backup RBs whose value transfers predictably.

The old-WR cliff is the worst bet on the board: the 10 oldest drafted players beat ADP just 30% of the time and old WRs only 21% — this year that's Adams and Evans — with encore-effect exceptions (Henry, Kelce, Stafford).

Tight end is elite-or-punt: pay for Bowers/McBride/Loveland/Warren or wait for late profiles with 17%+ target share and 15%+ air-yard share (Likely, Goedert, Kincaid, Juwan Johnson) — mid-round TEs waste RB/WR upside picks.

Middle-round RB and middle-round TE are the two worst-priced blocks on the 2026 board [FF/Jason] — 'the opportunity cost is too great' there this year. The paired swing: late-round QB has gone so far out of fashion that QBs are falling past their value, so the current edge is the middle-round QB, not the last-round one. Strategy rotates every couple of years as ADP self-corrects; the job is to find whichever block the market has mispriced THIS season, not to re-run last year's rule.

Sleeper-definition inflation [FF]. With ADP now accurate front-to-back and the average manager far more informed, a genuine sleeper can no longer be a known player at a modest discount — it has to be a player where 'right now it seems impossible' and the honest base rate is near-total failure. Corollary they apply on the same breath: late-round shots must go to players you believe are actually GOOD, because 'there are late-round guys who just stink' and opportunity alone on a bad player is a wasted ticket. This is the same bar our league_winners screen enforces.

Dynasty horizon is three years, not ten [FF]. They rejected their own 10-year 'who would you take' question on principle: player trajectories are not forecastable past ~3 years, so dynasty value should be argued on a three-year window. Directly relevant to our never-cut-youth rule — a young stash's thesis should be defensible inside three seasons, not on an indefinite 'someday'.
Never put an early-week (Wed/Thu) player in a FLEX slot; put him in his positional slot so the flex stays open to cover Sunday injuries or news.

Kicker selection: prefer a good kicker on a mediocre offense that settles for 40-60 yard field goals and rarely goes for it on 4th down; avoid kickers on aggressive TD-heavy offenses (DET, LAR, DAL) even if they're better real-life kickers.
Use Vegas player props (reception O/U) as a trustworthy read on a player's expected Week-1 usage; big money keeps those lines tight.
When a team refuses to say where a player's 'soreness' is, read it as PR cover for the previously injured joint (e.g. the knee for a two-time ACL back) — a red flag, not noise.
The days before Week 1 are the peak sell-high window for camp-hype players: benchmark offers against real trades happening in other leagues that week and convert hype into proven target-earners.
Draft capital a team spends to acquire a player reveals its valuation: a 2028 6th-rounder for Kaleb Johnson means RB3, not a real competitor.
Explosive-play seasons regress: 1,000 yards on ~84 targets (18% share) is not repeatable; target share is the sustainable driver (Saquon's 2024-to-2025 as the RB analogue).
A bad offensive line hits inexperienced running backs first; check consensus O-line rankings before buying a new RB1.
Historical base rate: no NFL running back has returned productive from back-to-back ACL tears; lean on the history rather than betting against it.
A QB returning from an Achilles loses downfield power (Cousins, Rodgers precedents), which specifically hurts his deep-threat WR while pushing volume to short-area TE/RB options.
A bottom-5 offense craters even elite-talent pass catchers (ARI 2025 with McBride/Harrison); QB situation can turn a 2nd-round WR into 5th-round value.
New-regime discount: a coaching staff with no draft-capital or money attachment to a player (Skattebo, 4th-round pick) will not force-feed him; check who the new staff signed.
Week 1 for last-round stashes is a usage read, not a points read: track snap share (75%+ = full starter), routes and targets, then either punt them on the first waiver wire or hold with conviction.

Depth-chart order does not predict who takes over after an injury; evaluate the more talented backup (Ollie Gordon over Jaylen Wright, Jonah Coleman over RJ Harvey, Vidal behind Hampton) rather than the listed RB2.

Prefer insurance backs with standalone weekly touches (Corum, Brooks, C-Rod, Monangai, Allgeier, Gainwell) over pure handcuffs; early-season handcuffs with zero standalone value cost you waiver churn.
Only ~24% of top-24 RBs survive 17 weeks — plan on injuries at RB and size handcuff/FAAB accordingly; but don't full-FAAB a backup on a bad offense (Miami) because he won't be a top-10 RB anyway.
Rookie WR base rate: non-high-first-round rookies start slow; only stash the ones projected for 75%+ snaps from Week 1.

TE age curve differs from RB/WR: tight ends are routinely fine at 31-33 (especially TD-dependent ones) without being Hall of Famers; athleticism matters more at TE than any position and TE breakouts often take 4-6 years.
Update conclusions when the data changes (court date moved two months = shorter absence); don't hold a take after its premise moves.
Last-pick IR trick: draft an IR-eligible player (Pacheco, Tyson) with the final pick, move him to IR, and add a free flier — an extra roster spot for nothing.
Week 1 tiebreakers: defenses are ahead of offenses so expect low totals; home favorites get the RB start/sit nod in coin flips; don't overreact to Week 1 results.
Ignore platform Week-1 projections and draft grades: platforms exist to run leagues, not to project players; historically an A grade is a warning and a D/F often means a great team.

Off-field/discipline risk in dynasty: discount a player whose value is team-specific (Rashee Rice) more than one whose skill translates anywhere (Nacua) — the latter gets paid by a WR-needy team even if his current team walks.
Players on the commissioner's exempt list can't go to IR — the stash costs a real bench spot for as long as the case runs.
